identification.summary: MalKamak is a name Cybereason gave to an Iranian threat group it says has been operating since at least 2018 and was first publicly reported in October 2021 [S1][S2]. Cybereason's Nocturnus and Incident Response teams tracked its activity as Operation GhostShell, an espionage campaign against aerospace and telecommunications firms [S1][S3]. The group's main tool is ShellClient, a previously undocumented RAT that evaded antivirus and used Dropbox for command and control [S1][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Cybereason: ShellClient development dates to at least November 2018; the vendor first responded to the activity in July 2021 and published in October 2021 [S1][S3][S5].
identification.notes: MalKamak is a Cybereason cluster name. Microsoft has no mapped name in this encyclopedia record. ETDA's threat group card, as summarized in search results, lists no alias other than MalKamak and Operation GhostShell as the campaign name, both from Cybereason [S7]. Cybereason notes possible links to Chafer (APT39) and Agrius but assesses MalKamak as distinct; these clusters are kept separate here [S2][S3].

attribution.sponsor: Iran, as assessed by Cybereason; ETDA's card, as summarized in search results, lists the group as state-sponsored [S1][S7]. No government attribution found.
attribution.confidence: Cybereason said it is confident, based primarily on code analysis, that MalKamak is an Iranian group [S5]. Cybereason described links to Chafer (APT39) and Agrius as possible but not enough for a firm link [S2][S3].
attribution.basis: Cybereason code analysis [S5]. Overlap with Chafer was shared credential-dumping and persistence methods. Overlap with Agrius was similar coding style and conventions, plus a ShellClient-associated domain that resolved to the same IP addresses as a domain used by Agrius's IPsec Helper malware. A Cybereason analyst speculated that a former member of Chafer or Agrius could now be involved, or that the three groups share tooling; this is speculation, not a confirmed link [S3].

objectives: Cybereason assessed the campaign aimed to steal sensitive information about critical assets, organizations' infrastructure and technology [S3]. Motivation is listed as information theft and espionage in ETDA's card, as summarized in search results [S7].

targeting.notes: Cybereason reported at least 10 affected organizations in the aerospace and telecom sectors, mostly in the Middle East with some in the U.S., Russia and Europe [S3][S6]. Individual victims were not named in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: ShellClient evolved from a basic reverse shell into a fuller espionage backdoor, with development dating to at least 2018 [S3][S5]. Version 4 is a modular PE using Costura to compress modules with zlib, and it stores most strings as bytes decoded at runtime to evade string-based detection [S5]. It profiles hosts (BIOS and MAC data, network details, installed antivirus, public IP via ipinfo[.]io) to derive a per-host agent ID [S5]. C2 uses the Dropbox API with an embedded key; data is AES-encrypted with a hardcoded key; victims poll a commands folder every two seconds and upload results to an agents folder [S5]. Persistence and SYSTEM privileges come from a service named nhdService, shown as Network Hosts Detection Service [S5]. Operators dumped credentials from lsass using an executable named lsa.exe that Cybereason suspects is a SafetyKatz variant but did not obtain [S4][S5]. Lateral movement used WMI, PAExec and net use [S4]. Initial access vector was not identified in the sources gathered.

campaigns.summary: Cybereason published Operation GhostShell, naming MalKamak and detailing ShellClient's Dropbox-based C2 and at least 10 victims in aerospace and telecom across the Middle East, U.S., Russia and Europe.

diamond.adversary: Iranian group MalKamak per Cybereason, with possible but unconfirmed ties to Chafer and Agrius [S2][S5].
diamond.capability: ShellClient RAT (Costura/zlib modular build, byte-encoded strings), lsa.exe credential dumping, WMI/PAExec/net use lateral movement [S4][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Dropbox accounts and API used as C2 with AS and CS folders; a ShellClient-associated domain shared IP addresses with an Agrius IPsec Helper domain [S3][S5].
diamond.victim: At least 10 aerospace and telecom organizations, mostly Middle East, plus U.S., Russia and Europe [S3][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Espionage collection on critical assets, infrastructure and technology of aerospace and telecom firms [S3][S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints with antivirus that relied on signatures/strings, and permissive egress to cloud storage such as Dropbox [S5].

gaps: Initial access vector is not stated in the sources gathered.
The Cybereason primary report could not be fetched (host unreachable from this environment); details rely on trade-press and search-result summaries of it [S1][S3][S5].
No reporting of MalKamak or ShellClient activity after October 2021 was found.
Victims are unnamed, and no government attribution or sponsor entity (for example IRGC or MOIS) is given.
Relationship to Chafer (APT39) and Agrius is unresolved; do not merge clusters [S2][S3].
MITRE ATT&CK has no group ID for MalKamak in this record; technique mapping not verified.
Version-by-version ShellClient evolution (2018 to v4) was not mapped in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Aerospace and telecom networks, and endpoints with permitted cloud-storage egress, are key terrain; aerospace firms overlap the defense industrial base [S3]. STEP 2: The actor operated undetected from at least 2018 until 2021 and relied on antivirus evasion and traffic blending with Dropbox [S3][S5]. STEP 3: Template is a persistent ShellClient service with SYSTEM rights, credential dumping from lsass, then lateral movement via WMI, PAExec or net use, with Dropbox C2 [S4][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued quiet collection against aerospace and telecom targets in the Middle East, U.S. and Europe. MDCOA, an assessment not stated by sources, is use of access in telecom or aerospace firms to support regional contingency planning. Candidate indicators: new service named nhdService (Network Hosts Detection Service), processes polling Dropbox API about every two seconds, outbound requests to ipinfo[.]io/ip from servers, and lsass access by unknown executables such as lsa.exe [S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track ShellClient indicators and Dropbox-abuse detections across DIB and telecom partners; the primary report's IOCs should be pulled by an analyst with access [S3]. (2) Authorities: blocking or monitoring cloud-storage egress on contractor networks depends on owner authority; coordinate through DC3 and DIB cybersecurity channels. (3) Mission assurance: telecom and aerospace dependencies may be exposed; identify supplier systems that support mission-critical networks. (4) Coordination: attribution is vendor-only and linkage to Chafer or Agrius is unresolved, so prioritize detection and containment over naming [S2][S3].

provenance.importedSummary: MalKamak is an Iranian threat actor that has been operating since at least 2018. They have been involved in highly targeted cyber espionage campaigns against global aerospace and telecommunications companies. MalKamak utilizes a sophisticated remote access Trojan called ShellClient, which evades antivirus tools and uses cloud services like Dropbox for command and control.
